w: The roof of the Sudetes: at 1,603 metres, Sniezka is the highest point in the Czech Republic, in Lower Silesia, in the Giant Mountains, and in the whole range - and the Polish-Czech border runs clean across its summit. One mountain, two countries, a single shared view.
s: The Sudetes' summit, straddling two countries
_facts: 1,603.3 m summit, highest point in the Czech Republic, Lower Silesian Voivodeship, Giant Mountains and the entire Sudetes
most prominent point of the Silesian Ridge in the Giant Mountains
lies on the border between the Czech Republic and Poland

w: Rogoznica was once the German village of Gross-Rosen, and the name still marks one of the Nazi camp system's darkest networks: at its 1944 peak, up to 100 subcamps spread across occupied Germany, Czechoslovakia and Poland, holding mostly Jewish, Polish and Soviet prisoners - 11 percent of everyone the system held.
s: A Nazi camp network in the Lower Silesian countryside
_facts: main camp in the German village of Gross-Rosen, now Rogoźnica, Lower Silesian Voivodeship
on the rail line between Jawor and Strzegom
prisoners mostly Jews, Poles and Soviet citizens
up to 100 subcamps at peak activity in 1944, 11% of all Nazi camp system inmates

w: Codenamed Riese - German for giant - this Nazi project dug seven underground structures at Ksiaz Castle and through the Owl Mountains in 1943-45, worked by forced labourers and camp prisoners, many of whom died building it. None were finished, only 11 percent poured in concrete, and nobody is certain what it was for.
s: Unfinished Nazi tunnels beneath the Owl Mountains
_facts: codename Riese, German for giant, 1943-1945 Nazi Germany construction project
seven underground structures at Ksiaz Castle and in the Owl Mountains, Lower Silesia
none finished, only 11% reinforced with concrete
purpose uncertain - possibly Fuhrer HQ and/or underground arms factory
built by forced labourers, POWs and concentration camp prisoners, many of whom died

w: Poland's only stave church didn't start here: built around 1200 in the Valdres region of Norway, it was dismantled, shipped east and re-erected in Karpacz in 1842. It still serves as a working Evangelical parish church, a stray Norwegian outpost standing in the Karkonosze foothills.
s: A Norwegian stave church, shipped to the Karkonosze
_facts: stave church in Karpacz, Karkonosze mountains, Poland
originally built c. 1200 in the parish of Vang, Valdres region, Norway
transferred and re-erected at its present location in 1842
Poland's only stave church, serves the Evangelical Church of the Augsburg Confession in Poland

w: A lone 718-metre granite peak rising out of the Sudeten foreland, its summit crowded with oddities: a PTTK mountain hut, a TV and radio mast, the Church of the Visitation of the Blessed Virgin Mary, and the barely-visible ruins of a castle. An observation tower tops it off, all inside a protected nature reserve.
s: A granite peak crowned with a church, ruins and a mast
_facts: 718 m granite mountain in the Sudeten Foreland, Poland, covered with forest
summit has a PTTK tourist hut, a TV/radio mast, the Church of the Visitation of the Blessed Virgin Mary, poorly visible castle ruins and an observation tower
peak protected as the Gora Sleza nature reserve, within the wider Sleza Landscape Park

w: Built under the terms of the 1648 Peace of Westphalia that ended the Thirty Years' War, the Church of Peace in Swidnica is the largest wooden Baroque temple in Europe - and still a working Evangelical-Augsburg parish today. It has stood on the UNESCO World Heritage list since 2001.
s: Europe's largest wooden Baroque church, built on a truce
_facts: largest wooden Baroque temple in Europe
built under the 1648 Treaty of Westphalia agreements ending the Thirty Years' War
belongs to the Evangelical-Augsburg Church in Poland's Swidnica parish
UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2001

w: Created in 1959 and now covering nearly 56 square kilometres of the Giant Mountains, this is Poland's half of a park that joined its Czech neighbour in 1992 to form a UNESCO transboundary biosphere reserve. Most of it is forest, but 40 hectares of peat bog earned their own Ramsar wetland listing.
s: Poland's slice of the transboundary Giant Mountains
_facts: national park in the Giant Mountains, Lower Silesian Voivodeship, created 1959
grew from 55.10 km2 to 55.76 km2, of which 17.18 km2 strictly protected, ~33.80 km2 forest
joined with Czech Krkonose National Park in 1992 as the Krkonose/Karkonosze Transboundary Biosphere Reserve
40 hectares of peat bogs designated a Ramsar wetland site

w: The Polish half of the Table Mountains, protected since 1993 across more than 63 square kilometres of Klodzko County, almost all of it forest. Its high point, Szczeliniec Wielki at 922 metres, gives the whole range its flat-topped silhouette, with a small strictly-protected core left untouched.
s: Table-top rock country in the Klodzko highlands
_facts: national park in the Polish section of the Stolowe (Table) Mountains, Klodzko County, Lower Silesian Voivodeship
created 1993, covers 63.39 km2, of which 57.79 km2 is forest and 3.76 km2 strictly protected
highest peak is Szczeliniec Wielki at 922 metres

w: Named for the Polish word for frost, Szrenica rises to 1,362 metres in the western Giant Mountains, its deforested summit given over to skiing on both the Polish and Czech sides. A weather station keeps watch near the top, inside Karkonosze National Park and close by the border.
s: A frost-named peak given over to skiing
_facts: 1,362 m peak in the western Giant Mountains, Poland, very close to the Polish-Czech border, within Karkonosze National Park
name derives from Polish 'szron' meaning frost
weather station near the summit; deforested slopes used intensively for skiing on both sides

w: Once rated a minor stronghold within the wider German Empire but one of Prussian Silesia's biggest, Klodzko Fortress is better known today for what's underneath: a sprawling tunnel network turned museum, its underground labyrinth stacked with everything from old fire engines to local glassware.
s: An underground labyrinth beneath a Prussian stronghold
_facts: fortification complex in Klodzko, Lower Silesian Voivodeship, Poland
once one of the biggest strongholds in Prussian Silesia, though regarded as minor within the whole German Empire
extensive network of tunnels forms an underground labyrinth, now a repository of objects from old fire engines to local glassware

w: Founded as a Benedictine house in 1242, run by Cistercians from 1289 until Prussia secularised it in 1810, then reclaimed by Benedictine exiles from Prague in 1919 - Krzeszow Abbey has changed hands about as often as the borders around it. Its Baroque basilica holds the mausoleum of the Piast dukes of Swidnica.
s: A Cistercian abbey that outlasted an empire
_facts: Baroque Cistercian monastery in Krzeszow, Lower Silesia, Poland; 1242 Benedictine foundation
run by Cistercians 1289-1810, secularised by the Prussian state in 1810
Benedictines from Prague took it over again from 1919
Basilica of the Assumption contains the mausoleum of the dukes of the Swidnica line of the Piast dynasty
designated a Polish official national Historic Monument (Pomnik Historii) on 1 May 2004

w: Bolkow Castle holds a 396-metre hill where the Nysa Szalona river has cut a sudden 90-metre drop on one side, while the other slopes gently down into the town below. The upland stronghold covers some 7,600 square metres, a hard-edged ruin northwest of Walbrzych.
s: A ruined stronghold on a river-cut hilltop
_facts: castle on Castle Hill in Bolkow, 396 m, where the Nysa Szalona river cuts a sharp 90 m precipice on one side
upland stronghold covering an area of 7,600 m2
located in Bolkow, 30 km northwest of Walbrzych, Lower Silesian Voivodeship

n: St. Stanislaus and St. Wenceslaus Cathedral
w: Swidnica's main Catholic church, dedicated to Saints Stanislaus and Wenceslaus - a historical monument standing at the heart of this Lower Silesian town.
_facts: historical monument and main Catholic building in Swidnica, Poland
also known as Swidnica Cathedral
